nesnd_civic_characters.102.d: Bellandi writes in the newspapers about the girls' school's finances, her pupils' families, and those whom poverty excludes from civic life. Under her questioning, the liberty and independence celebrated by republicans become matters of who pays the fees and who is allowed through the school doors.\n\nHer sympathetic readers cheer as one in print. But before women and the poor can truly walk into a classroom, someone has to pay for the school, and someone has to be willing to let them have the power that learning brings.
nesnd_civic_characters.103.d: Rusciani cannot discuss a common treasury for three sentences without coming back to the South's roads and schools. The political centre wants a dependable tax base; local traders want dependable trade routes. Everyone is for cooperation. The fight is over who pays first, and who carries the costs that keep piling up afterwards.\n\nMining revenue has become the fiercest point of all. Hand over your income first, then wait for others to decide whether to grant you any of it back? The South's taxpayers will not buy that.
nesnd_civic_characters.5.d: In the former papal lands, the dispute over education has spread from who may teach children to who will pay their fees. Vitali favours public contributions to school expenses and insists that local churches fulfil their educational responsibilities. This has made him unpopular even among some defenders of the Church's authority.\n\nThe Church wants to keep its schools, the government wants to raise citizens, and ordinary families just want their children to learn something useful. None of these wishes need clash; but the moment it comes to teachers' wages and poor pupils' fees, no one will part with a single coin more.
nesnd_civic_characters.107.d: Tong Shiheng's proposal ties the works to the merchants' interests. The ports want more goods from the interior, the merchants want a steady return on what they put in, and the towns want the road to reach their own doors. The three hopes sometimes run together and sometimes do not.\n\nSo the merchants' willingness to advance the money does not settle the argument. How long the concession runs and how its returns are shared will decide which works they are willing to start, and how much the towns will pay to move their goods for years afterwards.
nesnd_civic_characters.107.organisation: Port merchants and inland contractors are still seeking long concessions. Tong Shiheng's proposal for private advances would spare the government some ready cash, but traders along the routes fear they will pay far more in freight later.
nesnd_civic_characters.109.d: Bayantu insists that local negotiations follow the routes of migrating herds. Contractors can put a price on occupied land. Herders must work out where their animals can go once a passage is lost. If an alternative route lacks water and grass, a payment may do little to restore their livelihood.\n\nThese families ask that when the district does its sums, their lives be counted too.
nesnd_civic_characters.112.d: Guan Tingxian has brought the producing districts' demands into the budget debate. Oil companies want to use their returns to expand, while local traders need roads and schools for their businesses and families. If each distribution must wait until the companies have arranged their next investments, the districts will always receive what is left over.\n\nWhat he wants is not just a sum of money, but a voice for the districts when the money is shared out.
nesnd_civic_characters.114.d: Duan Jingchuan's concerns about the curriculum always return to his students' prospects. Academies can teach practical subjects, and local communities need these skills. Students also hope their knowledge will help qualify them to participate in affairs of state.\n\nThe classroom and the examination hall each weigh things differently, and the teachers are caught in the middle. The students' futures hang on qualifications; Duan fights for places and recognition so that what is taught in the classroom will count in the examination hall.
nesnd_civic_characters.115.d: Xu Tingzhang's opposition to arbitrary levies has found an echo among the local gentry. They will not willingly see their property consumed by post-war finances, or their qualifications diminished in the name of practical learning.\n\nYet local schools must still be run, and the army must still be paid. If the defenders of the old order want to go on running local affairs, they cannot simply list which funds may not be touched and which people may not be let in.
nesnd_civic_characters.116.d: Luo Yingtang begins her case for education with the accounts women workers know well. Being able to read wage slips and invoices gives them a voice in the workshop, and shows them they could take on other work. And so the demand for learning runs into the question of qualifications: once they have learned, what are they allowed to do?\n\nLiteracy teaching has spread from the workshops to the schools, but the old lines of status and qualification may not loosen with it.
nesnd_civic_characters.117.organisation: Employers want more skilled workers; workers want more pay once they are trained; and so the cost of the school is pushed back and forth between them. Han Shiduo once talked about education and wages in the same breath, and now the two quarrels have stayed in the workshops together.
nesnd_rg_aus_reason: The Hungarian question has been settled for now, but the arguing has not stopped. The scholars of Prague want schools of their own; the officials of Vienna want the provinces to carry out common policy to the letter. Provinces with different languages and interests still have to be held together, and Vienna must find a way to do it.
nesnd_rg_tur_reason: The Tanzimat has left laws and unfulfilled ambitions. Coastal merchants want to move their goods; provincial officials complain of inadequate revenues. If the country is ever to stop worrying about foreign debt and war indemnities, its ports, trade routes and provincial offices must actually work.
nesnd_rg_egy_reason: Cotton travels down the Nile to the coast, and foreign cloth comes back up from the ports. The army and the court tax this trade, but Egypt's craftsmen want workshops of their own. Build up schools, textiles and ports together, and Egypt will face the powers around it with a little more confidence.
nesnd_regional.1.d: Trains from Silesia bring coal and iron to Berlin, along with new petitions. The railway companies want the government to back trunk-line freight; the manufacturers want to build more machines and tools. The officers naturally favour more carrying capacity, though they have worked out a separate military use for every station.
nesnd_regional.2.d: Provincial schools are beginning to turn out a new generation of teachers and clerks. Some want them kept at home; others want them drawn into Vienna's bureaucracy. Both sides say they are serving the country. At bottom, the question is whether the money for education stays in the provinces, or the people who do the work go to the centre.
nesnd_regional.3.d: The port's shipping returns and the tax office's ledgers are starting to show what the investment has achieved. Merchants ask the government to keep its money in shipping; treasury officials say this is the moment to put the administration in order. Emergency levies are no way to run a country for long.
nesnd_regional.4.d: Egypt's workshops can now weave more of the country's cotton into cloth. The manufacturers want to expand production, but the schoolteachers warn the court that if reading and skills stay in the hands of a few, the new industries will soon run short of hands again.
nesnd_regional.5.d: The provincial schools, ports and workshops have all shown results. The state representatives want to keep the money flowing to the provinces; the government in the capital wants to use these achievements to shore up its authority.
nesnd_regional.6.d: Schools and transport in the South are showing some signs of life. Those who broke free of bondage want the chance to learn, and the business interests are urging the Union to keep supporting the railways. Abolishing slavery was only the beginning.
nesnd_regional.7.d: Railways now link part of the mining country to the coast, and Lima's merchants have begun to talk of bigger investments. The mine owners want to expand while the going is good; the engineers worry that without enough skilled men, the new machinery will simply stand idle.
nesnd_regional.8.d: This round of improvements was never finished as hoped. Schools, industry and transport are as pressing as ever, but the hopes that gathered around the programme have melted away. What was built still stands, and the promises that were broken are still remembered.
nesnd_regional_native_restoration_reason: Indigenous communities want their land in their own hands, and their own representatives running village affairs. The central government will not give up an inch of its authority. If the local councils can reach terms, all may yet live in peace; if not, it will mean independence and war.
nesnd_regional_native_war_reason: Indigenous communities have set up a separate government and are contesting the old government's right to rule. Who owns the land, whom the army obeys and what standing the communities will have are all staked on this struggle. Only when one side annexes the other will the divided rule end.
nesnd_regional_native.1.d: War has broken out between the Indigenous polity and the former government, and each demands the other's annexation.
nesnd_regional_native.2.d: The army has broken up the gatherings and scattered the leaders' networks. The Armed Forces approve, but resentment in the countryside has grown deeper still. Not one of the disputes over land and power has been resolved.
nesnd_regional_native.3.d: The opposing government's entire territory has been annexed by [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]. Divided rule is over; the local communities must now fight for their standing all over again under the new government.
nesnd_regional_native.4.d: The dispute is over, and we failed to annex our opponent. The local communities' demands for land and rights are still there.
nesnd_regional_native.4.a: We will take it one step at a time.
nesnd_regional_native.6.d: With the Indigenous polity fallen, people who fled their homes have arrived in [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName]. They bring their family ties with them, and demands that were never met.
nesnd_per_future_journal_reason: The rulers of the Tang-Persian court know the military government of Qin as well as they know Persia's merchants and great families. The Near-Western War brought them land and prestige, but the empire's direction is still undecided: push west with Ili's help, or use Western Qin's local troubles to strike east on its own account?
nesnd_per_civil_journal_reason: The offices brought in by the military government stand alongside local academies, religious schools and families. Getting officials of such different backgrounds to work under one roof needs reliable rules for appointment, and schools to train new men.
nesnd_per_economy_journal_reason: Cotton fields, weavers and passing caravans keep Persia prosperous. The court wants railways to join farms to towns, so that the lands won in the Near-Western War feed new workshops as well as the army.
nesnd_per.2.d: The craftsmen who came with the mission are now at work in our workshops, teaching surveying, building and the repair of machines. Whether these skills become lasting industries is up to our own workers and merchants.
nesnd_per.6.d: The court has formally asserted its claim to [SCOPE.sStateRegion('nesnd_per_claim_region').GetName]. The note has been delivered; who actually holds the land will still be settled by diplomacy or the sword.
nesnd_per.7.d: Our note on [SCOPE.sStateRegion('nesnd_per_claim_region').GetName] has been blocked by a great power. To win that recognition, we must first change the diplomatic situation there.
nesnd_per.4.d_unavailable: The court has settled on expansion westward, but the planned tributary pact with Ili has fallen through. The west can still be pursued; the troops and the money will simply have to be found by ourselves.
nesnd_per_governance_reason: The army wants pay, the towns want roads, and the schools and new laws are waiting for money too. The lingering glory of the Near Western War will not get any of it done. Ili can lend a hand, but whether the court stands firm depends in the end on our own schools, trade and peace at home.
nesnd_canon_diplomacy.1.alliance: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] wants a military alliance with us for a five-year binding period. Its envoy binds the safety of the German states to the continental order France dominates, and asks us to stand with them in diplomacy and on the battlefield from now on.
nesnd_canon_diplomacy.1.defense: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] proposes a defensive pact with a five-year binding period. What they want is an agreement that truly protects their independence: if either side is attacked, the other marches.
nesnd_canon_diplomacy.1.credit: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks France to stand guarantor for its Italian programme with six years of political credit. With French prestige behind them, its supporters can win over interests at home and abroad. The commitment does not touch the sovereignty of the Italian states.
nesnd_canon_diplomacy.1.investment: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] offers to open its market to our investors under an agreement with a five-year binding period. They want new factories and new expertise, and are ready to handle the scramble over profits that foreign capital brings. The agreement grants the right to invest; whether firms actually build depends on the business.
nesnd_canon_diplomacy.1.b: This is a commitment we cannot carry.
nesnd_canon_diplomacy.2.d: The other government has accepted the terms of our letter, and the agreed commitment now stands.
nesnd_canon_diplomacy.3.d: The talks came to nothing. Either the other side refused, or events changed during the negotiations and the original terms no longer held. The envoy returns empty-handed.
